questions.q: What is the main syntactic difference between `if`-`else` statements in C and Python?
choices: C marks the body statements with curly braces; Python uses indentation
C uses indentation to mark the body; Python uses curly braces
C requires an `else` part; Python makes it optional
C does not support chained `else if` branches
questions.explain: Python uses indentation to show which statements are in the body, and C uses curly braces. You should still indent C code properly so it is readable.

questions.q: In C, every `if` statement must have a matching `else` part.
questions.explain: The `else` part is optional, so a one-way branch (just `if`) is valid. The final `else` in an `if`/`else if` chain is optional too.

questions.q:
Given `int y = 5;`, what does this code print?

`if (y < 0) { printf("negative"); } else if (y != 0) { printf("positive"); } else { printf("zero"); }`
questions.explain: `y < 0` is false, so the next condition is checked. `y != 0` is true, so "positive" is printed and the rest of the chain is skipped.

questions.q: In a chain of `if` / `else if` / ... / `else`, when does the body of the final `else` run?
choices: Only when every earlier Boolean expression is false
Whenever the last `else if` expression is false
Always, after whichever branch was taken
When at least one earlier expression is false
questions.explain: The conditions are checked in order, and the first true one picks the branch. The final `else` runs only when all of the earlier expressions are false.

questions.q:
Given `int x = 3, y = 8;`, what is the value of `x` after this code runs?

`if (x >= y) { y = x; } else { x = y; }`
questions.explain: `3 >= 8` is false, so the else body runs and `x = y` sets x to 8. After this code, both variables hold the larger of the two values.

questions.q: Which of these integer values evaluate to true when used as a condition in C?
questions.explain: In a C condition, zero is false and any nonzero value is true, whether it is positive or negative.

questions.q: Which of these are relational operators in C?
questions.explain: The relational operators are `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, and `>=`. `!`, `&&`, and `||` are logical operators.

questions.q: Given `int x = 0;`, what happens when C evaluates `if ((x != 0) && (10 / x > 2))`?
choices: The condition is false, and `10 / x` is never evaluated
The program divides by zero because both operands are always evaluated
The condition is true because 0 counts as true
C evaluates the right operand first, so it divides by zero
questions.explain: `&&` short-circuits. The first operand is false, so the whole expression has to be false and the second operand is never evaluated.

questions.q:
Given `int a = 1, b = 5;`, what is the value of `b` after this statement?

`if ((a == 1) || (b++ > 0)) { }`
questions.explain: `||` stops at the first true operand. `a == 1` is true, so `b++ > 0` is never evaluated and b stays 5.

questions.q:
Given `int x = 5, y = 7;`, what is the value of `x` after this code runs?

`if ((x > 10) && (y >= x)) { x = 13; } else if (((-x) == 10) || (y > x)) { x = y * x; } else { x = 0; }`
questions.explain: `x > 10` is false, so the first `&&` is false. In the else-if, `-5 == 10` is false but `y > x` (7 > 5) is true, so `x = y * x` gives 35.

questions.q: C's logical and (`&&`) stops evaluating at the first false operand, and logical or (`||`) stops evaluating at the first true operand.
questions.explain: This is short-circuit evaluation. C stops evaluating a logical expression as soon as its result is known.

questions.q:
How many lines does this code print when `num` is 1?

`val = 1; while (val < num) { printf("%d\n", val); val = val * 2; }`
questions.explain: A `while` loop checks its condition before running the body. `1 < 1` is false, so the body never runs.

questions.q:
How many values does this code print when `num` is 20?

`val = 1; while (val < num) { printf("%d\n", val); val = val * 2; }`
questions.explain: It prints 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16. After that, val becomes 32 and `32 < 20` is false, so the loop ends.

questions.q:
What is the value of `val` after this loop finishes?

`int val = 1; while (val < 100) { val = val * 2; }`
questions.explain: val doubles through 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. When val is 128, `128 < 100` is false and the loop ends.

questions.q: A `do`-`while` loop always executes its body at least once.
questions.explain: A `do`-`while` loop runs the body first and checks the condition afterward, so the body always runs at least once.

questions.q:
How many lines does this code print?

`int n = 5; do { printf("%d\n", n); n++; } while (n < 3);`
questions.explain: The body runs once and prints 5 before the condition is checked. Then `6 < 3` is false, so the loop stops.

questions.q: Which of these is correct C syntax for a `do`-`while` loop?
questions.explain: The body comes after `do`, then the condition in parentheses after `while`, and the statement ends with a semicolon.

questions.q: Which C keyword starts a loop that runs its body before checking its condition?
questions.explain: In `do { ... } while (cond);`, the body comes first and the condition is checked afterward.

questions.q: What order does C use to evaluate `for ( <initialization>; <boolean expression>; <step> ) { <body> }`?
choices: initialization (once) -> boolean expression -> body -> step -> back to boolean expression
initialization -> body -> step -> boolean expression -> back to body
boolean expression -> initialization -> body -> step, all repeated on every iteration
initialization -> step -> boolean expression -> body -> back to step
questions.explain: The initialization runs once. Then C repeats this cycle: evaluate the condition (and leave the loop if it is 0), run the body, evaluate the step.

questions.q: In `for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) { printf("%d\n", i); }`, how many times is the initialization `i = 0` evaluated?
questions.explain: The initialization is evaluated only once, when the loop is first entered.

questions.q:
What is the value of `i` after this loop finishes?

`for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) { printf("%d\n", i); }`
questions.explain: After printing 2, the step sets i to 3. Then `3 < 3` is false and the loop ends, so i is left at 3.

questions.q:
What is the last value printed by this loop?

`for (i=0, j=0; i < 10; i+=1, j+=10) { printf("i+j = %d\n", i+j); }`
questions.explain: On every iteration j equals 10*i, so i+j equals 11*i. The last iteration has i = 9, which gives 99.

questions.q: How many times does the body of `for (i = 10; i < 3; i++) { ... }` run?
questions.explain: The condition is checked before the first run of the body. `10 < 3` is false, so the body never runs.

questions.q: In `for (i=0, j=0; i < 10; i+=1, j+=10)`, what separates the multiple statements in the initialization and step parts?
questions.explain: Commas separate statements inside one part. Semicolons separate the three parts (initialization, condition, step) from each other.

questions.q: In C, any `while` loop can be written as a `for` loop, and any `for` loop can be written as a `while` loop.
questions.explain: In C, `for` and `while` loops are equally powerful, so any loop written with one can be written with the other.

questions.q: Which `for` loop is equivalent to `int guess = 0; while (guess != num) { ...read a new guess... }`?
questions.explain: The initialization sets guess to 0 and the condition is `guess != num`. The step is left empty because the body reads a new guess.

questions.q: Which C loop is the more natural fit for repeating until the user enters an even number (an indefinite loop)?
questions.explain: Either loop can do it in C. A `while` loop is the more natural fit for indefinite loops, and a `for` loop is the more natural fit for definite loops such as iterating over a range of values.

questions.q: Python's `for` loop iterates over a sequence of values, but C's `for` loop is a general looping construct with initialization, condition, and step parts.
questions.explain: That is why C's `for` loop can express indefinite loops like the guessing loop. In Python, that kind of loop has to be written with `while`.
